subject: Chemistry
title: How Yeast Makes Bread Rise
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on How Yeast Makes Bread Rise.

hook.text: Yeast cells eat sugar and exhale carbon dioxide. Those tiny gas bubbles are what make bread fluffy.

buildup.text: Saccharomyces cerevisiae—baker's yeast—converts glucose into CO₂ and ethanol through anaerobic fermentation.

discovery.text: The CO₂ gets trapped in the gluten network. As the dough proofs, bubbles expand and the dough doubles in size.

twist.text: The ethanol evaporates during baking. So bread dough technically makes alcohol—but the oven burns it all off.

climax.text: Sourdough uses wild yeast and lactobacillus bacteria. The bacteria produce lactic acid—that's the sour tang.

punchline.text: Yeast eats sugar, exhales gas. Bubbles trapped in gluten. Bread rises.

quiz.question: What gas does yeast produce that makes bread rise?

details.summary: Yeast ferments sugars in dough through anaerobic respiration, producing carbon dioxide gas and ethanol. The CO2 bubbles become trapped in the gluten network, causing the dough to rise. The ethanol evaporates during baking, while the Maillard reaction creates the golden crust.
details.whyItMatters: Yeast fermentation is one of the oldest biotechnologies, dating back over five thousand years. Understanding its chemistry has enabled modern industrial baking and the craft bread renaissance.
takeaways: Yeast converts sugar to carbon dioxide and ethanol anaerobically
Trapped CO2 gas creates the airy structure inside risen bread
The Maillard reaction between sugars and amino acids browns the crust

faq.question: Why does bread dough need to rest and rise before baking?
faq.answer: Resting allows yeast to multiply and produce enough carbon dioxide to create the desired airy texture. It also allows gluten strands to relax and develop a flexible network that can stretch around gas bubbles. Rushing the process produces denser, less flavorful bread.

faq.question: Why does bread taste different from the raw dough ingredients?
faq.answer: Fermentation produces hundreds of flavor compounds including organic acids, esters, and aldehydes. The Maillard reaction during baking creates additional complex flavors. Longer fermentations, like sourdough, produce more acids and aromatic compounds, explaining their distinctive taste.
